A B S T R A C T
Few-shot fine-grained image classification remains a challenging task due to the subtle inter-class variations
and the scarcity of labeled data. Existing few-shot fine-grained methods often struggle to generalize effectively
under low-data regimes and fail to discriminate between visually similar samples. To address these challenges,
we propose DistillCvT, a two-stage framework to enhance model generalization and feature discrimination
through self-supervised learning and self-distillation within prototypical network structure. Convolutional
Vision Transformer (CvT) is employed as the feature extractor, which integrates convolutional locality with
transformer-based global modeling to capture fine-grained details while preserving global context. DistillCyT
mitigates these issues through a two-stage strategy. In the first stage, the model is trained using a prototypica
distance-based classification loss, where class probabilities are computed from the distances between query
samples and class prototypes, complemented by standard data augmentation to mitigate data scarcity and
learn discriminative class representations. In the second stage, an identical student model is trained with
a self-supervised jigsaw task to enhance feature discrimination and robustness by aligning support samples
with their augmented query counterparts. Simultaneously, the teacher model from stage one guides it through
logit-based self-distillation to further improve generalization. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, Stanford Dogs,
and Stanford Cars demonstrate that DistillCvT consistently improves performance and achieves competitive
results compared with recent state-of-the-art few-shot fine-grained image classification methods.

often lack flexibility to generalize to unseen tasks [6–8]; optimization-

are prone to overfitting [9–11]; and metric-based approaches, which
learn a feature embedding space by comparing distances between query
samples and support examples [12–14]. Among these, metric-based
methods have become especially popular due to their simplicity, effi
ciency, and strong performance in few-shot settings. However, existing
methods often rely on static similarity measures and employ backbones
that either prioritize local features or global context, thereby overlook
ing sample-specific discriminative cues and limiting their effectiveness

To address these limitations, we propose DistillCvT, a two-stage
metric-based framework that integrates self-supervised learning and
self-distillation to improve generalization and feature discrimination for
FS-FGIC. Unlike conventional backbones, Convolutional Vision Trans-
former (CvT) [15] is employed as the feature extractor. CvT extends the
standard Vision Transformer (ViT) [16] by incorporating convolutional
projections in both token embedding and attention layers, enabling bet
ter preservation of spatial locality while maintaining global modeling
capacity. It also introduces a hierarchical architecture with progres-
sive downsampling, similar to CNNs, while retaining the flexibility of
transformers. Although CvT provides strong local–global representa
tions, adapting it to few-shot fine-grained classification is challenging,
as transformers generally require large-scale training data and are
prone to overfitting in low-data regimes. DistillCvT mitigates these
challenges through a principled two-stage learning strategy. Specif-
ically, CvT captures both subtle local details and global contextual
relationships that are crucial for fine-grained recognition, while the
second stage combines self-supervised learning and self-distillation to
address the limited-data nature of FS-FGIC. The self-supervised ob-
jective enhances part-aware and semantically consistent representa-
tions under spatial perturbations, whereas self-distillation regularizes
the learning process and reduces overfitting. Together, these com-
ponents form a complementary framework that simultaneously im-
proves feature discrimination and robustness in low-data fine-grained
classification.
In the first stage, CvT is trained from scratch using standard data
augmentation to increase data diversity and learn robust local–global
representations. In the second stage, a jigsaw-based self-supervised
objective is introduced to regularize representation learning without
requiring additional labels. Specifically, an identical student model is
trained with spatially permuted query images, encouraging the extrac
tion of discriminative local cues that remain informative despite spatial
perturbations, while support samples serve as pseudo-classes. Simul-
taneously, a self-distillation process is applied, where the pretrained
teacher model from the first stage guides the student through its logits.
By jointly leveraging jigsaw-based self-supervision and teacher–student
distillation, DistillCvT learns more discriminative and generalizable
representations for few-shot fine-grained image classification.

ford Cars demonstrate that the proposed DistillCvT achieves consistent
performance improvements in both 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios. The

2. Related work
2.1. Model-based methods
Model-based methods aim to develop adaptable learning mech-
anisms for few-shot fine-grained image classification across diverse
datasets and tasks. Wu et al. [6] propose a bi-directional reconstruc-
tion framework to improve class separability and feature consistency,
while Cheng et al. [17] introduce DFR to disentangle discriminative
features from class-irrelevant variations. Attention-based approaches,
such as TWA [18], guide the extraction of task-specific and comple-
mentary object representations. Other studies enhance feature learn-
ing through cross-modal distillation [7], second-order pooling [19],
pose-normalized representations [8], and deep object parsing [20].
Although effective, these methods often depend on carefully designed
architectural components or structural priors, which may limit their
adaptability and generalization in highly data-scarce scenarios.
2.2. Optimization-based methods
Optimization-based methods focus on improving adaptation to new
tasks by modifying the training process or feature optimization strat-
egy. Zhou et al. [9] design a graph neural network-based optimizer to
enhance embedding adaptation across tasks. Other approaches intro-
duce auxiliary mechanisms to improve feature learning, such as atten-
tion optimization for discriminative region focusing [10], cross-feature
refinement [11,21], and self-optimal transport for improved matching
and grouping [22]. Feature reconstruction-based methods [23] further
enhance spatial consistency while suppressing irrelevant information.
More recently, FHNet [24] incorporates frequency-guided hierarchi-
cal optimization to better capture both local and global fine-grained
patterns. Despite their effectiveness in adapting to new tasks, these
methods remain prone to overfitting under extremely limited training
data.
2.3. Metric-based methods
Metric-based methods aim to learn an embedding space where
samples from the same class are closer than those from different
classes. Recent approaches enhance feature discrimination through
multi-scale attention and feature alignment mechanisms, including
DLG [25], FFSNet [12], BSNet [26], TDSNet [27], and foreground
alignment strategies [28]. Attention-based metric learning has been
further explored in TDM [29], HelixFormer [30], BFGL [31], Fec-
Net [32], and Attention-Guided Pyramidal Features (AGPF) [33] which
utilize task-specific attention, multi-level feature learning, and support-
query alignment to capture discriminative local representations. To
improve similarity modeling, existing methods employ cosine similar-
ity [34], non-linear projection metrics [35], part-aware learning [36],
saliency-guided distillation [14], and query-guided feature weight-
ing [37]. Reconstruction-based approaches further enhance feature
consistency and discrimination through self-reconstruction [13], bi-
directional reconstruction [38], cross-reconstruction [39], channel-wise
attention-enhanced mutual reconstruction [40], and cross-sample fea-
ture interaction [41]. In addition, interactive triplet attention [42]
models complementary spatial and channel interactions to capture
subtle fine-grained differences. Despite these advances, existing metric-
based methods often rely on predefined similarity measures and may
struggle to fully exploit sample-level discriminative information under
extremely limited training data.

and transformer-based architectures to improve feature discrimination
and generalization under limited training data [24,40–42]. In the

stages: (1) Supervised Training, where a teacher model is trained from
scratch to learn strong local–global feature representations; and (2)

The two-stage design is adopted to facilitate effective
self-distillation. In the first stage, the teacher model is trained under
the few-shot learning objective to learn reliable task-specific repre-

provides informative soft targets for student optimization in the second
stage. This decoupled training process enables effective knowledge
transfer while allowing the student to simultaneously benefit from

3. The DistillCvT framework
Fig. 1 illustrates the overall architecture of the proposed Distill
CvT framework, developed under the few-shot learning paradigm with
an 𝑁-way 𝐾-shot setup. The framework consists of two sequential
stages: (1) Supervised Training, where a teacher model is trained from
scratch to learn strong local–global feature representations; and (2)
Self-Supervised Distillation, where a jigsaw-based self-supervised task
improves representation robustness and a logit-based self-distillation
mechanism transfers knowledge from the teacher to a student model,

The two-stage design is adopted to facilitate effective

the few-shot learning objective to learn reliable task-specific repre-
sentations and class relationships. The resulting teacher subsequently
provides informative soft targets for student optimization in the second
stage. This decoupled training process enables effective knowledge
transfer while allowing the student to simultaneously benefit from
self-supervised learning.

unseen test classes, and the average classification accuracy with a 95%
confidence interval is reported to ensure statistical reliability.

To evaluate the generalization capability of DistillCvT, the learned
embedding space is visualized using t-SNE on the Stanford Dogs dataset
under the 5-way 1-shot setting. Five novel test classes, each with
100 samples, were randomly selected: Weimaraner, Komondor, French
bulldog, Pomeranian, and Pembroke. Fig. 2 (left to right) compares
embeddings from (1) the baseline model, (2) with standard augmenta-
tion, (3) with SSL, and (4) with self-distillation. To quantitatively assess
the clustering quality across these stages, Table 3 presents the Davies–
Bouldin Index (DBI) values for each configuration. A lower DBI score
indicates more compact intra-class clustering and better inter-class sep-
aration, reflecting superior clustering performance. The baseline model
(1) exhibits severe class overlap, reflected by a high DBI of 171.247.
The introduction of standard augmentation (2) mitigates this scattering,
reducing the DBI to 81.563. The addition of the SSL module (3) yields
a substantial improvement in class boundary delineation, dropping the
DBI dramatically to 5.303. Finally, the full DistillCvT model with self-
distillation (4) produces the most highly discriminative feature space,
achieving the lowest DBI of 4.935. These qualitative and quantitative
enhancements progressively demonstrate that self-distillation improves
generalization while self-supervised learning enhances representation
robustness.

4.6.2. Attention rollout
In hybrid architectures such as Convolutional Vision Transform
ers (CvT), conventional gradient-based visualization methods often
produce diffuse activation maps because the global interactions intro-
duced by deep self-attention layers tend to weaken spatial correspon
dence [73]. To better understand the model’s decision-making process,
we employ Attention Rollout on the deepest semantic stage, allow-
ing us to trace how information is propagated through the attention
lavers. As shown in Fig. 3. the baseline CyT model is highly suscepti
ble to background distraction, with attention frequently spreading to
irrelevant regions such as tree branches and surrounding structures
instead of focusing primarily on the target object. In contrast, the
proposed DistillCvT exhibits a more concentrated attention pattern,
emphasizing the most discriminative regions of the object while sup-
pressing responses from irrelevant background regions. These visual-
izations confirm that DistillCvT enforces a highly robust, object-centric
feature representation and exhibits reduced sensitivity to contextual
distractions.

perturbations. This regularization effect helps the model focus on subtle

layouts. Such robust feature learning is particularly beneficial in few-

5. Conclusion
This paper presents DistillCvT, a two-stage framework that inte-
grates self-supervised learning and self-distillation to improve feature
discrimination and generalization for few-shot fine-grained image clas-
sification. Built on the Convolutional Vision Transformer (CvT) back
bone, which combines convolutional locality with transformer-based
global modeling, the framework is designed to capture both local
and global representations crucial for fine-grained recognition. In the
first stage, CvT is trained from scratch using standard data augmen-
tation to enhance data diversity and representation robustness. In the
second stage, a student model with an identical architecture lever-
ages a jigsaw-based self-supervised objective that encourages semantic
consistency under spatial perturbations, promoting the extraction of
robust local discriminative features without requiring additional anno-
tations. Simultaneously, a self-distillation process is employed, where
the pretrained model from the first stage acts as a teacher to transfer
task-specific knowledge to the student model, thereby reducing overfit
ting and preserving global semantic information. By jointly leveraging
self-supervised learning and self-distillation, DistillCvT demonstrates
the effectiveness of training CvT in low-data regimes. Experiments on
three benchmark datasets show that DistillCvT achieves competitive
performance compared with existing methods in few-shot settings.
Future work will explore adaptive region-level augmentation and cross
modal supervision to further improve fine-grained discrimination and
advance data-efficient learning in computer vision.
